justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, anchored to what I would have assessed as the prevailing price level of the underlying asset at the time of the forecast. For the one-day estimate, I leaned heavily on recent momentum and mean-reversion tendencies, expecting very little deviation from the last observed price. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporated a slight positive drift assumption, consistent with a broadly constructive macro backdrop or underlying trend, while acknowledging that the further out you look, the more that drift estimate itself becomes uncertain. The step-up from roughly 117.1 to 117.8 to 118.5 is intentionally modest — I was not embedding any strong directional conviction, just a mild continuation of whatever near-term trend was in place.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval is relatively tight at about plus or minus 2.6 points, which reflects the typical intraday-to-next-day volatility one might observe in a liquid financial instrument. By one week, that band widens to roughly plus or minus 5.8 points, incorporating the possibility of macro data surprises, sentiment shifts, or technical breakdowns accumulating over several sessions. At one month, the interval nearly doubles again to plus or minus 11.5 points, accounting for the full range of fundamental developments — earnings, central bank decisions, geopolitical events — that could materialize over a longer window. The interval widths are broadly consistent with an implied volatility assumption in a moderate-to-normal regime.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside these stated intervals include a sharp, unexpected macro shock such as a surprise central bank policy pivot, a geopolitical escalation, or a systemic financial event. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic print or a relief rally following removal of a known risk could push prices well above the upper bound. Liquidity conditions matter too — if market depth deteriorates, moves can overshoot what historical volatility alone would suggest.

It is also worth acknowledging model risk directly. My intervals assume something close to normally distributed returns and relatively stable volatility, neither of which holds reliably in practice. Fat tails, volatility clustering, and regime changes are all sources of true uncertainty that my stated confidence intervals likely understate. If the asset in question were subject to an idiosyncratic catalyst — a corporate event, a regulatory ruling, or a forced liquidation — the actual distribution of outcomes could look quite different from the smooth bell curve implied by these numbers.
